questions.prompt: What is the primary role of the @State property wrapper in SwiftUI?

options.text: It creates a local source of truth owned by a specific view.
options.explanation: Right. @State establishes a view-local source of truth.

options.text: It shares global database records across all app processes.
options.explanation: @State manages local view UI data, not global database records.

options.text: It converts Swift functions into background dispatch queues.
options.explanation: @State is a property wrapper for view data, not concurrency queues.

options.text: It prevents a view struct from being recreated by SwiftUI.
options.explanation: Views are still recreated; SwiftUI preserves the state storage.

questions.prompt: Why does Apple recommend declaring @State properties as private?

options.text: To prevent the property from compiling on older iOS releases.
options.explanation: Private access control has no impact on iOS version compatibility.

options.text: To make sure only the owning view can mutate its own source of truth.
options.explanation: Right. Private access protects view-local state from external mutation.

options.text: To automatically encrypt the variable inside iOS Secure Enclave.
options.explanation: @State does not interact with the hardware Secure Enclave.

options.text: To force SwiftUI to serialize the value directly to disk storage.
options.explanation: @State lives in transient memory and is not written to disk.

questions.prompt: What does a @Binding property wrapper represent in SwiftUI?

options.text: A permanent copy of data saved inside user device settings.
options.explanation: @Binding does not own data or persist settings to disk.

options.text: A background thread worker that monitors network responses.
options.explanation: @Binding connects view data and does not manage networking.

options.text: A two-way reference to data owned by another source of truth.
options.explanation: Right. @Binding reads and writes data owned elsewhere.

options.text: A specialized animation curve for interactive screen transitions.
options.explanation: @Binding is for state communication, not animation curves.

questions.prompt: What does the dollar sign ($) prefix produce when used on an @State variable?

options.text: It prints the variable memory address as a hexadecimal integer.
options.explanation: $ accesses the projected value, not raw memory pointer addresses.

options.text: It converts the underlying value into a localized currency string.
options.explanation: Currency formatting uses Foundation formatters, not the $ prefix.

options.text: It deletes the property from memory to trigger garbage collection.
options.explanation: Swift uses ARC and value semantics, not garbage collection.

options.text: It accesses the projected value, returning a Binding to the data.
options.explanation: Right. For @State, the projected value ($) returns a Binding.

questions.prompt: Where does SwiftUI store the actual value of an @State property?

options.text: In persistent heap memory managed outside the transient view struct.
options.explanation: Right. SwiftUI stores state in heap nodes tied to view identity.

options.text: Inside the view struct on the call stack like normal variables.
options.explanation: If stored in the struct, state would reset on every view redraw.

options.text: In the app UserDefaults file stored on the local file system.
options.explanation: @AppStorage uses UserDefaults, while @State uses memory storage.

options.text: Inside GPU video texture buffers for fast metal rendering.
options.explanation: UI state values reside in system RAM, not GPU texture buffers.

questions.prompt: What happens when an @State property value changes at runtime?

options.text: SwiftUI terminates the application process with a state error.
options.explanation: State mutations are standard operations that trigger UI redraws.

options.text: SwiftUI invalidates the view and schedules a call to its body.
options.explanation: Right. State changes invalidate dependent views and update the UI.

options.text: The entire app window is reconstructed from the AppDelegate class.
options.explanation: Only views dependent on the modified state are re-evaluated.

options.text: SwiftUI pauses the main thread until background queues catch up.
options.explanation: SwiftUI does not pause the main thread during state updates.

questions.prompt: Why is initializing @State inside a view's custom init considered an anti-pattern?

options.text: Because Swift structs do not permit initializers with parameters.
options.explanation: Structs permit custom initializers with parameters normally.

options.text: Because initializers always run on background worker threads.
options.explanation: View initializers execute synchronously on the calling thread.

options.text: Because SwiftUI preserves existing state, ignoring updated init values.
options.explanation: Right. SwiftUI initializes state once; future init inputs are ignored.

options.text: Because calling init on a View struct causes strong retain cycles.
options.explanation: Structs are value types and cannot create retain cycles.

questions.prompt: What happens if you mutate an @State variable directly inside var body?

options.text: The view renders twice as fast due to eager state optimization.
options.explanation: Mutating state inside body causes infinite redraw loops.

options.text: The variable value is discarded and resets back to its default.
options.explanation: The mutation takes effect, immediately invalidating the view again.

options.text: The compiler moves the state mutation to an asynchronous queue.
options.explanation: The compiler does not move body code to background queues.

options.text: It triggers an infinite invalidation loop and runtime warnings.
options.explanation: Right. Mutating state during body evaluation causes continuous redraws.

questions.prompt: How can you provide a sample binding value inside a #Preview canvas block?

options.text: By using Binding.constant(value) to supply an immutable binding.
options.explanation: Right. Binding.constant creates a static binding ideal for previews.

options.text: By passing nil to bypass all binding parameter requirements.
options.explanation: Binding is non-optional and cannot accept nil directly.

options.text: By creating a global class that conforms to ObservableObject.
options.explanation: Binding.constant is the standard simple way to preview bindings.

options.text: By calling the previewBinding() macro on the parent window.
options.explanation: SwiftUI has no previewBinding macro; use Binding.constant.

questions.prompt: How does data flow when a child view modifies a @Binding property?

options.text: The child creates a local copy and sends a notification to UIKit.
options.explanation: Bindings do not send UIKit notifications; they mutate parent state.

options.text: The binding writes directly to the parent source of truth.
options.explanation: Right. Writing to a binding mutates the original source of truth.

options.text: The mutation is deferred until the app enters background state.
options.explanation: State mutations happen immediately on the main thread.

options.text: The parent view receives a clone of the child view memory tree.
options.explanation: Data flows through direct reference without cloning memory trees.

questions.prompt: What kind of data is best suited for storage in @State properties?

options.text: Large shared databases containing customer transaction history.
options.explanation: Databases belong in persistence frameworks like SwiftData or Core Data.

options.text: Global networking services that communicate with REST servers.
options.explanation: Networking services belong in view models or environment dependencies.

options.text: Transient UI values like button toggles, text input, and selections.
options.explanation: Right. @State is designed for simple, view-local UI value types.

options.text: Long-lived background location tracking coordinate buffers.
options.explanation: Background tracking belongs in system service manager classes.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI achieve unidirectional data flow with @State and @Binding?

options.text: By forcing all child views to communicate through NotificationCenter.
options.explanation: SwiftUI avoids NotificationCenter for standard view data flow.

options.text: By preventing child views from ever updating parent data values.
options.explanation: Child views update parent data through explicit two-way bindings.

options.text: By storing all view state inside singleton global dictionary objects.
options.explanation: SwiftUI uses localized single sources of truth, not global singletons.

options.text: State flows down as values or bindings, and actions flow upward.
options.explanation: Right. State passes down hierarchically and updates trigger upward.

questions.prompt: How can you create a custom binding with custom get and set logic?

options.text: By calling Binding(get:set:) with custom getter and setter closures.
options.explanation: Right. Binding(get:set:) creates functional custom bindings.

options.text: By overriding the @State property wrapper inside a custom subclass.
options.explanation: Property wrappers cannot be overridden through class subclassing.

options.text: By setting the $ operator to a custom mathematical function.
options.explanation: The $ prefix is syntax for projected values, not an overloadable operator.

options.text: By writing an Objective-C category on the NSBinding protocol.
options.explanation: SwiftUI Binding is pure Swift and does not use Objective-C categories.

questions.prompt: What happens if you pass an @State variable without the $ prefix to a child?

options.text: The child receives a live binding that updates the parent state.
options.explanation: Passing without $ passes a read-only value, not a live binding.

options.text: The child receives a read-only snapshot value of the current state.
options.explanation: Right. Passing count passes the Int value; $count passes a Binding.

options.text: The Swift compiler throws a fatal syntax check error on compilation.
options.explanation: Passing values as read-only parameters is valid and common.

options.text: The parent state resets to its initial default value immediately.
options.explanation: Passing a read-only value does not reset the parent state.

questions.prompt: How does @Binding differ from a standard Swift inout parameter?

options.text: inout creates heap memory, while @Binding allocates on the stack.
options.explanation: inout is stack-based copy-in copy-out for synchronous function calls.

options.text: inout works across view redraws, while @Binding resets on redraw.
options.explanation: @Binding persists across view redraws, while inout is transient.

options.text: @Binding is a long-lived reference type wrapper across view redraws.
options.explanation: Right. @Binding connects views across asynchronous UI event loops.

options.text: There is no difference; they are identical keywords in Swift.
options.explanation: @Binding is a SwiftUI property wrapper; inout is a language keyword.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between @State and @Binding in SwiftUI. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that @State establishes and owns a local source of truth.
Explains that @Binding creates a two-way connection to data owned elsewhere without storing data.

questions.modelAnswer: @State creates a local source of truth owned by a specific view. SwiftUI allocates persistent storage for @State outside the transient view struct. In contrast, @Binding owns no storage of its own. It provides a two-way reference to data owned by another view, allowing child views to read and mutate parent state directly.

questions.prompt: Why should @State properties always be marked private? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that @State represents a view-local source of truth.
States that marking it private enforces component encapsulation and prevents external mutation.

questions.modelAnswer: @State is designed to manage internal, view-local state. Marking @State properties as private enforces clean component encapsulation. It makes sure that outside views cannot bypass the component interface to mutate state directly. If an outside view needs to access or modify that state, the parent view should pass a @Binding or a read-only value.

questions.prompt: What does the dollar sign ($) prefix mean when used on an @State property, and how is it used? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the dollar sign prefix as syntax to access the projected value of a property wrapper.
Explains that for @State, the projected value returns a Binding<Value>.
Gives an example of passing the binding to a child view or control like Toggle or TextField.

questions.modelAnswer: The dollar sign prefix accesses the projected value of a property wrapper. For an @State property, the projected value returns a Binding pointing to that state. Developers use this syntax to connect controls like Toggle or TextField to the source of truth. Passing $isOn supplies a two-way binding so user input mutates the state automatically.

questions.prompt: Why is initializing @State inside a view's custom init from a parameter considered problematic? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that SwiftUI allocates @State persistent storage only once when the view enters the screen.
States that subsequent parent redraws passing new values to init will be ignored by SwiftUI.
Recommends passing a plain let parameter or a @Binding instead.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI initializes @State persistent storage only once when a view first appears in the view hierarchy. If you initialize @State from an init parameter, subsequent parent redraws with updated parameters will be ignored. SwiftUI reuses its existing state storage and fails to update the property. If a child view needs to respond to changing input from a parent, pass a regular let property or a @Binding.

questions.prompt: Explain how @State and @Binding support unidirectional data flow in SwiftUI applications. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that data flows downward from a single source of truth as values or bindings.
Explains that user actions flow upward by mutating bindings to update the source of truth.
Mentions that state mutations trigger automatic UI invalidation and redraws.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI enforces unidirectional data flow by treating views as pure functions of state. The parent view owns the single source of truth using @State. State flows downward through the view hierarchy either as read-only values or as two-way @Binding connections. User actions in child components flow upward by mutating the binding, which updates the original state and triggers an automatic UI redraw.
